job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents on their farm outside Alderwick, about twenty minutes from town. I'm up at six to feed the hens before I open my laptop. I spend the morning on applications and an online course in power systems, and in the afternoon I help my dad with whatever's seasonal, hay or fencing. Evenings I sing in the church choir twice a week, and my fiancé Jonas calls from his apprenticeship two counties away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. Tell me about your degree and internship.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electrical power engineering at Stanmore University. My final project was a small wind turbine for farm use, which powered a water trough in the trial field for three weeks before a bearing failed. I also spent ten weeks at a regional power company, shadowing the substation maintenance crew. I'd like a graduate job in power distribution or renewables, close enough to come home on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about right. New things rarely do everything the salesman claims, and on the farm we've seen that with every gadget. I'd tell my friends from choir that there's no need to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own situation is the problem, not the technology. There are plenty of utilities and contractors near Alderwick, but they hire graduates in the spring intake, and I missed it. My savings are fine and my parents are happy for me to stay, but Jonas and I want to marry in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the next intake and ring the substation crew I met, in case something opens. I'd also finish the power-systems course. And I'd help my dad more, because a farm always has work, and I'd rather be busy than just waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Nothing is wrong, but I want to start my life, and it's on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Jonas and you want to marry in two years. How does the job hunt fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've decided that I need a job before we set the date, and he needs his apprenticeship finished. So we're both waiting on something, and neither of us enjoys it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family feel about the delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum says good things come in time, and Dad says nothing, which is his way. I know he'd like me to be settled.

I'd tell my choir friends there's no need to worry.

Help Dad on the farm to stay **busy**.
feel: **Uneasy**: nothing is wrong, but my life feels on hold.

Finish the power systems course by Christmas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change we should handle carefully, and that churches and families should help people through it. I'd say that employers who train their own young people will do best, and I'd say it at the next choir supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think entry-level design and paperwork in power companies goes to software first. Field work, the substations and lines, stays for people, at least for a while. So more of the jobs I'd take are on the outdoor side, which actually suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd target operations, maintenance and field engineering roles, and I'd ask for a place on the substation crew. I'd use AI tools more at work for the planning and reports, once colleagues show me. And I'd save more so Jonas and I can still put down a deposit on a cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. I've got family and savings, but a wedding on one income is a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI tools more once colleagues show you. Why wait for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not against them, I just don't trust a thing until someone who's used it for a few months says it earns its keep. That's how my dad buys a tractor too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding date if the search drags on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the date but make it smaller. Jonas's family would help with the hall, and I'd do the flowers myself.

say: It's change to **handle carefully**, and churches and families should help people through it.
Employers who train their own young people will do best.
think: Entry-level design and **paperwork** go to software first, while field work stays longer.
That suits me, since the **outdoor side** of power work is where I'd rather be.

Save more for a **deposit** on a cottage.

steps.text: Apply for substation maintenance and field engineering roles

Plan a smaller wedding with family help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is far too fast and I'd say it plainly. I'd say that no government should allow something this big without families and communities having a say, and that we need to protect people who work with their hands and their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it frightens me. I trained for thinking work, so I'd be hit early, and Jonas's apprenticeship has about the same three more years as hands-on work does. Then we'd both be exposed at around the same time, in 2031. I don't see how we afford a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job in power, maintenance or the farm co-op, and work for my dad full-time if I had to. I'd put the wedding and the house on hold and save every spare pound. I'd also ask the church about people who've been through something like this, because we have a few elders who started again from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the one where my plans fall apart, and I can't see how to rebuild them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the wedding on hold. How would Jonas react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say no at first, because he's a stubborn romantic. But he'd see it, and we'd do the church part and the party later. A marriage matters more than the reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want the government to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep a basic income for people who lose work, protect small farms and trades, and make large firms pay a share. I don't love handouts, but I'd take this one over doing nothing.

We need to protect people who work with their hands and heads.
think: I trained for thinking work, so I'd be hit **early**, and Jonas would be exposed around **2031**.

S2.quote: A marriage matters more than the reception.
fieldNote: Her fear **centres** on the shared plans with Jonas, not herself alone.
Asks church elders for lived **experience** of starting again.

steps.text: Take any power, maintenance or farm co-op job
Put the wedding reception on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is workable if people take it seriously. I'd say we should be building local training, with churches, farms and small firms at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's roughly fine, though uneasy. I could be married, have a first job, and put some savings away before 2031. The thinking side of power work is exposed, but field work holds until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job in power or renewables as soon as I can, preferably in the field. I'd marry as planned and rent near Jonas's work. I'd put half our spare money into the cottage deposit. And I'd learn drones for line inspection, because I think that's a job that grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. There's a plan, and it's one I'd like to follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why drones for line inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's an outdoor job where a human still decides what matters, and the power companies already use them. It also means I get to walk the fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas's younger brother, who's about to start an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick the trade where you need to be on site, learn the tablet side as well, and save from your first wage. That's the advice I'd have wanted.

Churches, farms and small firms should help build local training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a good amount of time. I'd say that people should use it to build their lives and their skills, and that governments should help families and small firms, not wait for them to fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's calm, with a bit of watchfulness. By 2036 I'd be thirty-three, married, with children maybe, and a decent career in the field. The thinking side will be done by machines but the physical work holds until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a normal first job and build up a good record. I'd marry and buy the cottage. I'd keep learning, including the AI tools, once they're settled, and I'd think about running a small renewable-energy firm for farms with Dad as a first customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I could live with that decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a small firm for farms. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a seed. Farms need solar and small wind that someone local installs and fixes, and nobody does it well near us. I'd test it on weekends first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry you might be too trusting that things will be fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But worrying a decade ahead doesn't pay the bills. I'd rather plan and adjust.

say: Ten years is a **good amount of time** to build our lives and skills.
Governments should help families and small firms, not wait for them to fail.
think: For me it's **calm** with some watchfulness: married, a career and maybe children by 2036.
Thinking work goes to machines, but physical work holds until about **2039**.
do: Take a normal **first job** and build a solid record.
Test a small **renewable-energy** installation firm for farms on weekends.
feel: **Calm**: I could live with that decade.
S4.quote: Farms need solar and small wind that someone local installs and fixes, and nobody does it well near us.
fieldNote: Time turns her **family-first** plan into a small business idea.
Remains **watchful** without letting worry rule her.

steps.text: Take a first job and keep a solid record

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though not for the reasons you'd think. It's the wedding, the house and the farm that keep me up. Everything I'm planning with Jonas rests on two incomes, and two years doesn't give us time to build that. What would help is steady employers who hire locally, and a community that looks after its own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe just that people think farm kids are behind the times. We use new things all the time, we just pick the ones that pay for themselves.

headlineQuote: People think farm kids are behind the times. We use new things all the time, we just pick the ones that pay for themselves.
portrait: Tara is a **23-year-old** electrical power engineering graduate living on her parents' farm, engaged to Jonas, and still without an offer.
She is **traditional** and values family, faith and work, and she backs free markets and apprenticeships over handouts.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and takes up new things once they pay for themselves, so she adjusts steadily.
Her mood is **uneasy** or anxious in most worlds, because her wedding and house plans depend on two incomes.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her wedding, house and two-income plans need more time than that.
whatWouldHelp: Steady employers who **hire locally** and a community that looks after its own.
